1 · Goal, scope and how the unit runs

GoalGet the shape of task management right before 0.1.0: what a task, a board, a run and a routine are; how planning and running are kept apart; how work starts; and the screens that follow from it. One model, simple enough for a first user to understand without reading anything.
Why a unit of its ownIt changes the core of the product, its data and the agents’ tools, so it is architecture, not triage. Owner: “this is going to change everything about task management, which is the whole point of our platform … this is a release blocker as well, but … needs its own unit and careful thinking … a milestone.”
In scopeTasks (states, the task page), boards (custom fields, boards as views, sprints), runs (the execution state, the Runs views, one place for what needs you), how work starts (Run, Start per agent, Run at…, agents), routines (as repeatable runs), and the Tasks, Boards, Runs, Your tasks screens.
Not in scopeConversations and the model a conversation uses (its own release blocker); places, files, workspaces; the Fleet Console; true custom fields beyond the one type a board uses (later).
Blocksagenthix@v0.1.0. Opened after the triage unit is paused and merged.
How this board is usedIt is the input to the unit’s spec: the problems (u2), what is decided (u3), the words (u4), the requirements (u5), the model (u6), what changes (u7), and what is still open (u8). The explorations that led here (R0–R0h) and the Runs proposals (R1–R8) stay below as reference.

2 · What is wrong today

#ProblemSeen where
P1Tasks competes with Runs. The Tasks list counts run states (Needs you, Running, Waiting), which is Runs’ job; planning and running are mixed.4b walk, 7 Nov (your words)
P2A board’s column sets the task’s state. Moving a card changes whether the task is done; a board can’t simply describe a project’s own steps.board.md; R0e
P3A task is on exactly one board. Moving it to another board drops its place on the first, with no record there.ADR-0097; R0c
P4A sprint is locked inside one board, so the sprint can be seen only through that board’s columns.board.md (Sprints); R0d
P5Work starts in too many hidden ways: a column that starts work, the automation switch, the pulse, the throttle, the queue limit, start times, routine rounds. Hard to understand.automation.md; R0h (your words)
P6Routines are tied to tasks: a routine makes a task per round and that task starts itself.routines.md; your words
P7No project Backlog. Ideas not yet placed have nowhere to sit but some board’s Backlog.ADR-0097; your words
P8Runs are shown in three places that disagree, say a run’s state three ways, and hide why a run waits, what it cost and who started it.R1–R8 (design pass captures)
P9What needs you is scattered: Your tasks, the rail’s Runs panel and the task lists each count it.R0 (Your tasks vs the Runs panel)

3 · Decisions

#DecidedYour words (7 Nov)
D1Tasks plan; Runs carry the plan out. A board is where a set of work is arranged; Tasks, Boards and Runs are overviews.“task is for the user to plan … the execution side is the run”; “the actual work happens on the board … task list, board list and run list all show aggregate”
D2Three kinds of state, never derived from each other: the task state (To do · In progress · Done; built in; set on the task), the execution state (set by the system from the task’s runs), and the project’s custom fields.“i dont think we should marry it to the task state … done always means done … they all mean different things”
D3A board is a saved view. Built in: Task state (all types, by state) and Execution. Any other board shows one task type’s columns, or one custom field’s options, with an optional filter (sprint, epic, agent).“there is always a board for the task state and a board for the execution state”
D4Custom fields are extra views. A custom field has a type; only single select is built now. A task can have a value in many, so it can be on many boards; they never touch the task state.“a custom field that is compatible with the board view is what we need for flexibility”
D5Only a task type’s columns set the task state, through the state each column sits in. A custom field never does.“i dont think we want to map a custom field to a done state” → then “maybe custom field that has single selection can have an option that ties it to a single task state?” → task types (D10)
D6A task starts only by an explicit act: a person’s Run on one task, Start on an agent in the project’s Runs (its ready tasks: To do, not yet run, one at a time in rank order) or Start all agents (every agent in the project), or Run at… (the task’s start time); or an agent starting it with its tool. No column, option, switch or background pulse starts work. Automation is agents (and, later, routines’ runs) starting work explicitly.“the auto start feature was a remnant of the old heartbeat flow … we just need a way for user to define when the task gets picked up”
D7A routine is a repeatable run, with its own runs, not linked to tasks by default; creating tasks is something its run may do.“a routine is just a repeatable thing, a repeatable run … regardless of whether it has a task or not”
D8A sprint is its own concept, a time box on the project; a sprint board is any board filtered to the current sprint.“so sprint is no longer a board it now has its own concept”
D10Task types, each with its own columns. A project has one or more task types (e.g. Task, Bug, Feature request); each type has its own columns, and each column sits in one task state. A task has one type and is in one of its columns; its state follows from the column. Every project starts with a type Task whose columns are the four states. Boards are views over a type’s columns, the task state, the execution state or a custom field. (Not “workflow”: that word is the script library’s.) Changing a task’s type keeps its state.“we do several per project the point is to get the architecture right or it will be hard to change after release … a task type … each task type can have their own work flow … these are the state that maps directly to the task state”
D11Backlog is the first task state: Backlog · To do · In progress · Done. A new task starts in Backlog.“we should have a backlog state … easier to reason about”
D12An epic is a built-in task type in every project: never run, but it may have an agent who manages it (talks it through, writes and orders its tasks); replaces the isEpic flag.“yes ok”
D13One sprint series per project, one cadence for every type.“1 sprint series per project”
D14One rank per task, project-wide: every board sorts by it; it is the order an agent’s Start follows.“yes i agree”
D15A routine is a schedule, an agent, instructions and an optional model, in a project or a person’s own space, on behalf of the last person who changed it. Each firing starts one run (a routine run, shown in Runs); it creates or starts tasks only through its agent’s tools; each routine is on or off.“yes. that looks right.”
D16Task types are defined per project, from Library templates; organisation-wide types later. Linked tasks come later.“defined per project … org wide types later”; “not now, its too complex”
D17Work starts per agent, from the project’s Runs. Each agent has ▶ Start (its ready tasks, rank order, a confirm with ticks) and ■ Stop; the header has Start all agents (every agent in the project, each on its own ready tasks) and Stop every run. Boards only arrange the work; a single task is run from its page or a card’s ⋯.“maybe we attach the run to a single agent instead? and run all to all agents? so then the context is on the agent not on the task”; “yes”
D18The agent’s avatar shows the run. Wherever a task has an assigned agent (a card, a list row, the task header, a line in Runs): Waiting = a thin dotted ring; Running = a turning ring; Needs you = a full ring with a dot badge; Failed = a full ring with a ! badge; Not started and Finished = no ring. On cards and rows the ring replaces the run marker (words on hover); the task header keeps its words.“show a circular progress indicator around the agent’s avatar if it is queued for running … the avatar double up as a running state indicator”; “yes please”
D19Workrooms, Workroom and Runs. Each project’s Workroom shows its agents at work as scorecards (its main room; smaller rooms come later); HQ’s Workrooms (in the rail) shows every project’s Workroom on one page; Runs is the history list, separate from both, at both levels.“command centre inside a hq… does that still make sense?”; “Alright yes lets do workrooms”
D20The rail has eight places in three groups, with a divider between them: Home · Chat · Your space | Projects · Your tasks · Workrooms | Agents · Library. Boards, Workspaces and Routines across projects become tabs on the Projects page (undoing 4a’s rail places).“it might get too much for the user”; “yes … update it - also consider adding a left panel divider for each of the 3 concepts”
D21One Markdown editor, everywhere text is written: a task’s description, comments, a routine’s instructions (and any new place). Built once in @agenthix/ui (today’s MarkdownBox, lifted and used by every caller).“any markdown editor [should be] reused everywhere - that includes the task description, comment, and routine instructions”
D22A routine’s schedule is a cron expression with a timezone, so it can do everything cron allows; people build it from presets in words (every N minutes or hours, daily, weekdays, weekly, monthly on day N or the first/last weekday) or type any cron in Advanced; it is read back in plain words with the next three run times; no more often than every 5 minutes. HQ’s one scheduler (ADR-0088) keeps ticking every minute and reads each routine’s cron rule (its next due time stored), rather than a cron job per routine.“do we support everything cron job allows?” → “yes i agree”
D9Your tasks is your planned work across projects; what needs you lives in Runs only.“yes i think so”

4 · The words

WordWhat it is
TaskOne piece of work: what, why, who, by when. It has one task type, one column of its type (so one task state), a rank, at most one sprint, values in any custom fields, and runs.
Task stateBacklog · To do · In progress · Done. Built in, the same in every project; it is the state of the task’s column. Done always means done.
Task typeA kind of work in a project (Task, Bug, Feature request, Epic), with its own columns. Every project has Task and Epic.
ColumnOne of a task type’s own named columns (e.g. Accepted, Building, Testing), sitting in one task state. A task is in one. On a board grouped another way, the columns are the states or a field’s options.
EpicThe built-in type that groups tasks toward one goal; never run.
BoardA saved view of the project’s tasks in columns: one type’s columns; the task state across types; the execution state; or one custom field’s options. With an optional filter.
Custom fieldA field the project defines; only single select now. An extra view; never sets the task state.
RankA task’s place in the project’s one order; every board sorts by it.
SprintA numbered time box in the project’s one series. A task is in at most one.
BacklogThe first task state: wanted, not yet committed to.
RunOne go of an agent, until it hands back: a task’s run, a reply in a conversation, a routine’s run.
Execution stateWhat an agent is doing with a task now, from its latest run: Not started, Waiting, Running, Needs you, Failed, Finished.
An agent’s lineThe tasks started for one agent in a project, taken one at a time, in rank order.
RoutineA schedule, an agent and instructions; each firing is one run.

5 · The states a task has

What a task hasValuesSet byAnswers
Type and columnOne task type; one of that type’s columns (e.g. Feature request: Submitted · Accepted · Building · Testing · Shipped)People and agents, by moving its card on its type’s board, or setting its columnWhere is it in this kind of work?
Task state · built inBacklog · To do · In progress · Done: the state its column sits inFollows its column; setting the state directly lands on that state’s default columnHas it been committed to, is it under way, is it finished? Done always means done
Execution state · built inNot started · Waiting · Running · Needs you · Failed · FinishedThe system, from the task’s latest runWhat is an agent doing with it right now?
Custom field valuesFor each single-select field: one option, or none (shown as Not on this board)People and agentsExtra views; never the task state
SprintOne sprint of the project’s series, or nonePeople and agents; Finish sprintWhich time box is it planned in?
RankIts place in the project’s one orderDragging on any boardWhat comes next?
ArchivedYes or noPeople and agents; the done-task sweepIs it out of sight?

Backlog means work someone wants but hasn’t committed to doing (as in Scrum, Jira and Linear). It is the first task state, so the project’s Backlog is simply the tasks in it, on every board and in every list; a new task starts there. Moving it to To do is deciding to do it. Planning a sprint takes tasks from Backlog or To do into the sprint.

6 · Requirements

A board

Purpose. Arrange one set of work in its own columns, and start it in the order I choose.

#As a user, I want …so that …
B1to see every task in its column, with how many in eachI see where work piles up
B2to drag a task between columns and reorder within onethe board says where each piece is and what comes next
B3to put the work in order by dragging cardseach agent takes its ready tasks in that order when it is started (Runs)
B4to see on a card, only while it matters, that it is running or needs meI can act without leaving the board
B5to filter a board to a sprint, an epic or an agentone board serves several slices
B6to talk the board through with an agent, and have it add and order tasksI don’t type tasks myself

Boards

Purpose. See every board in the project and how each is going.

#As a user, I want …so that …
BS1each board’s spread across its columns at a glanceI spot the one that is stuck
BS2to make a board from a field (or a new field), or from a Library templatea new kind of work gets its own columns

Tasks

Purpose. Find and plan any task in the project.

#As a user, I want …so that …
T1counts by task state, and what is late or has no agentI know where the plan stands
T2one line per task with its fields (each field a column I can show), epic, agent, due dateI can compare and plan
T3to search, filter and sort by any of them, with no fixed groupingI choose the slice
T4the project Backlog in viewI decide what to plan next
T5each epic with its progressI see what goes together

Runs (a project’s, and across projects)

Purpose. See the plan being carried out, and answer what needs me.

#As a user, I want …so that …
RU1what needs me first: approvals, questions, failuresno agent waits on me longer than it must
RU2each agent’s line: running now and its step, up next, why it waitsI know the work is moving
RU3what finished, its result and its costI can check the work and the spend
RU4to start an agent on its ready tasks, or every agent at once, and to stop an agent or a runwork starts and stops by agent, from one place
RU5task runs, replies in conversations and routine runs, with a way to narrow to one kindnothing running is hidden

A task and a run

Purpose. Everything about one piece of work; everything about one go of an agent.

#As a user, I want …so that …
TK1approved in 4b (task-stories 1–11): where it stands, does it need me, its result, its runs, change course, organise itthe task page stays as approved, with its fields and sprint added
RN1a run’s steps, model, site, time against its limit, and costI see what it did and what it cost

Your tasks

Purpose. My planned work across projects.

#As a user, I want …so that …
Y1the tasks I own or that my agents hold, across projects, by due dateI plan my week

Routines (designed in this unit)

Purpose. Repeat a run on a schedule.

#As a user, I want …so that …
RT1to say “every weekday at 9:00, do this”, with an agent and its instructionsrepeating work needs no task each time
RT2to see each routine’s runs like any other runI know it ran and what it did

8 · What changes

AreaWhat changes
Data (hq)Task: gains typeId, stepId, rank; status becomes state with Backlog first, written from its step; loses boardId, column, isEpic, routineId, roundAt. New TaskType and TypeColumn (each project gets Task and Epic). CustomField, FieldOption, TaskFieldValue for extra views. Board becomes a view (kind, type or field, filter); loses its columns JSON, sprints, Show also. Sprint moves to the project. Routine reshaped (schedule, agent, instructions, model, on behalf of, on/off). Automation settings, the throttle and RUN_THROTTLED go. Site: AgentRun.routineId. Clean slate: nothing converted.
Starting work (hq)The pulse, the throttle, the queue limit, the automation switch and the column that starts work are removed (hq/src/automation/: pulse, roundState, queueNotes…; projects/autoQueueColumns.ts, taskRunMoves.ts; about 17 files name autoQueue, 23 the throttle). Kept: each agent’s line, start times, run limits, the site’s limit on runs at once. New: Start and Stop per agent, and Start all, on the project’s Runs (D17).
Epics (hq)An epic may have an agent again (4b refuses one: “Unassign its agent first”); it is still never run: Start, Start all agents and Run skip it.
Routines (hq, site)A routine fires on its schedule and starts one run of its agent with its instructions (D15); no task per round. The scheduler keeps firing routines and start times (Run at…) only.
Agents’ toolscreate_task, update_task, change_tasks, list_tasks, get_board, list_boards, open_board, create_board, finish_sprint, rename_sprint, run_task, create_routine, update_routine: reworded for fields, views, sprints on the project, and how work starts. Tool descriptions checked on the baseline model.
Client protocolThe task and board shapes the browser and the mobile app receive change: a version move with deprecation marks (docs/architecture/versioning.md).
ScreensA board; Boards; Tasks (scorecards and columns); a task’s Details (fields, sprint, state); Runs (project, the rail’s panel, the Runs page; R1–R8); Your tasks; a project’s Sprints; making a board and a field; Routines; the Automation tool and Manage › Settings › Automation (removed or reduced).
DocsConcepts: tasks/task.md, board.md, automation.md, routines.md, agents’ execution flow; the user guide’s task, board and automation pages; QA scenarios.
Decision recordsNew records replace ADR-0097 (a board is a lasting workflow), ADR-0087 (work starts on its own only from automation), ADR-0088 (one scheduler) in part, ADR-0091 (depth) depending on u8, ADR-0092 and ADR-0104 (routines and their rounds).
TestsIntegration tests of the board, sprint, automation and routine services; the cross-app suite where runs start; e2e for every screen above.

9 · Questions answered

#QuestionRecommendedTag
Q1Can an agent start a task?Yes (owner, 7 Nov: “It has to be. How else will we automate”). Its limits: Q1a.decided
Q1aThe limits on an agent starting a taskAs today: on behalf of the person its run is for (ADR-0095), in its run’s project, depth bounds chains (ADR-0091), recorded as the agent’s. Only the queue limit goes (it served the pulse).existing
Q2One sprint series per project, or several?One per project, one cadence for every type (owner, 7 Nov).decided
Q3How are cards ordered on boards?One rank per task, project-wide; every board sorts by it, dragging on any board changes it; the Execution board is not dragged (owner, 7 Nov).decided
Q4What is a backlog, and where does it fit among the states?Backlog is the first task state: Backlog · To do · In progress · Done (owner: “I agree … easier to reason about”). See U4b.decided
Q10Should a field’s options carry a task state?Through task types (owner, 7 Nov): each type’s columns each sit in one task state; moving a card sets the state; other single-select fields never do. See D10.decided
Q11Are task types defined per project, or by the organisation?Per project, made from a Library template; organisation-wide types later, for reuse (owner, 7 Nov).decided
Q12Is an epic a task type?Yes: a built-in type in every project, never run, with columns like any type; replaces the isEpic flag (owner, 7 Nov).decided
Q5Is Project Tasks replaced by the built-in Task state board?Yes: follows from D3; a task needs no board.follows from D3
Q6Does a finished run change the task state?No, as today: a run ending leaves the task’s state alone; a person, or the agent with its tool, moves it.existing
Q7Routines: what a routine’s run does, on whose behalf, and tasksDecided: D15 (owner, 7 Nov).decided
Q8Do linked tasks (blocks, waiting on) come in this unit?Not now: too complex; the basics first (owner, 7 Nov). Additive later, no migration.decided
Q9Who may define custom fields and boards?As today: anyone who may work in the project may make a board and its columns (requireMayWorkInProject); the same for fields.existing

How they are drawn.
  • Wireframes in the style of R0b, whole screens, numbered and keyed, each with Before (today, or the earlier proposal) and After.

A project’s Tasks: the plan, counted by task state Approved

wireframe · planning

What this asks. The project’s list of every task, drawn from the new model: scorecards count the task state (Backlog first), never the runs; each line shows its type and the column it is in; any field can be a column; the default order is the project’s one rank. T7 (approved in 4b) is kept where it still fits: one line per task, chips beside the title, filters as chips, epics as rows with a ring. Approve, or say which numbers you’d change.

Before

24 · today: fixed groups Needs you · Up next by run state; Backlog and Done as buttons that leave the page; “Board · column” cut.

T7, approved in 4b (built)

What each number is, and why

1Scorecards by task state, plus Late and No agent
All · Backlog · To do · In progress · Done · Late · No agent. A card is also the quick filter. No run states anywhere: no Needs you, Running or Waiting card.		T1, T4; P1 (Tasks competed with Runs); D1, D9 (what needs you lives in Runs). Backlog first, D11.
2Talk about tasks
An agent can make, order and change tasks for you; the conversation opens beside the list.		“I probably just end up getting the agent to do that for me” (story 17); B6’s counterpart for the whole project.
3Filters as chips, as T7
＋ Filter: Type, Column, Task state, Epic, Sprint, Agent, Priority, a custom field, Archived. Each in use is a chip with ✕.		T3. Type and Sprint are new (D10, D13).
4Sort, default Rank
Rank is the project’s one order, the same every board sorts by. Also Priority, Due date, Recently updated, Newest. T7’s Importance goes: it put what needs you first, which is Runs’ job now.		T3; D14 (one rank); D9.
5Any field can be a column (Fields ▾)
Column, Agent and Due are shown by default; Sprint, Priority and every single-select custom field (here Launch stage) can be added. The choice stays on this list for you.		T2: “each field a column I can show”. Custom fields are views only (D4): shown, never the state.
6The column, and the run on the agent’s avatar
The column the task is in (Fixing), by name only: its task state stays out of the list (owner, 7 Nov); the scorecards count by state. The agent’s avatar carries the task’s run as a ring: dotted for Waiting, turning for Running, a dot for Needs you, a ! for Failed, none when not started or finished. Its words show on hover (drawn once, on WEB-14). No chip, no count		D10; D18 (the avatar shows the run), the same ring on the board’s cards, so a task reads the same everywhere.
7One line per task, its type first
The type’s mark, the title, then chips: priority, epic, sprint. Under it: key, type, who it came from, when it last changed. An epic is a line like the rest with its ring (3 / 5), as T7.		T2, T5; D12 (Epic is a type). The board name leaves the line: a task belongs to no board (D3).

Left open

  1. Dragging a row when sorted by Rank: does it change the rank, as dragging a card on a board does? Recommended: yes, only while sorted by Rank; with any other sort the rows have no handle. One rank, so the list and every board agree (D14).
  2. Does a click on the ringed avatar open the run in Runs? Recommended: yes, when it has a ring; otherwise the click opens the task like the rest of the line.
Why.
  • Owner, 7 Nov (4b walk): “tasks are competing with the runs screen. Because the scorecards are showing the execution states”.
  • T7 (approved 6 Nov): no fixed grouping, scorecards that filter, chips over columns except agent and state, epics with a ring.
  • Spec §6 T1–T5; §3 D1, D4, D9, D10, D11, D14.

What each number is, and why

1The project’s Backlog is a card
Backlog is the first task state (D11), so the project’s Backlog is the tasks in it, whatever their type: a Bug in Reported, a Feature request in Submitted, a Task in Backlog. Manual order, the order an agent’s Start follows (Runs).		T4; D11, D14; P7 (no project Backlog today). Answers R0b’s open item 5.
2Act on a selection
Tick lines, then Move to To do (each lands on its type’s default To do column), Add to sprint…, Set epic…. Nothing starts work: running is on a board or a task.		T4: decide what to plan next; D6 (only an explicit Run starts work); D13 (a sprint takes tasks from Backlog or To do).
3Epics, with progress by task state
The ring counts the epic’s tasks that are Done; the line under it counts the rest by state. Sorted by due date for planning.		T5; D12. T7 counted needs-you here; that is Runs’ now (D9).

Left open

  1. Is Move to To do on a selection worth it, or is dragging on a board enough? Recommended: keep it: the list is where the Backlog is triaged across types, which no single type’s board shows.
Why.
  • T7’s planning view (approved 6 Nov): “see the progress of each … sort by importance or maybe the date of the epic”.
  • Spec §5: “Planning a sprint takes tasks from Backlog or To do into the sprint”.

What each number is, and why

1The board’s name, and a switch to another saved board
‹ Boards goes back to the list (Saved boards); the name opens the other saved boards, so moving between Bugs and Feature requests is one click.		D3: a board is a saved view; BS1 is the list.
2Columns: one control, four ways to plan
Here: Bug’s columns. The same control groups by the task state, another type’s columns, a custom field or the execution state (drawn on Board by task state, by custom field and by execution state). Changing it changes only what you see until you save (Saving a board).		Owner: “one board view but with those as different ways to plan the work”. D3, D10.
3Filters: Sprint, Epic, Agent, and search
Each a button that becomes a chip with ✕ when set (Board filters). Search hides cards that don’t match; nothing on the board changes.		B5. Search kept from 4c B1; B1’s Priority and Needs you only filters go: what needs you lives in Runs (D9).
4Only the column’s name
A column shows its name and count, never the task state behind it: that is defined once, in Settings › Task types (Task types), with the type’s columns.		Owner, 7 Nov: “only show the column name not the task state … hide that complexity away … if they create a new column they should define it elsewhere.”
5Cards are in rank order; there is no Sort
Top to bottom by the project’s one rank. Dragging a card up or down changes its rank, on every board.		D14, Q3: one rank, project-wide; every board sorts by it.
6Drag to move and to order
Dropping a card in another column sets its column, and so its task state; dropping it between two cards sets its rank. The dashed slot says where it lands before you let go. A move never starts work.		B2, D5, D6: only a type’s columns set the state, and no column starts a run (4c B3’s “Starts a run” column is gone).
7Starting work: the project’s button, and one task’s
▶ Start all agents… in the header is the project’s button, the same as in the Runs header (Workroom): it starts every agent in the project on its ready tasks (To do, not yet run) in this rank order, after one confirm, whatever this board’s filters. No run button on a column. One task runs from its page or a card’s ⋯ (Run); one agent from its station on Runs.		Owner, 7 Nov: boards arrange the work and its order; starting moves to Runs. D6, D14.
8The agent’s avatar shows the run
A ring round the agent’s avatar, only while it matters: a thin dotted ring while Waiting, a turning ring while Running, a full ring with a dot when it Needs you, a full ring with “!” when it Failed. Not started and Finished: no ring. The words (Running · 3 min · writing the fix; 2nd for Writer; the question; the error) show on hover, drawn here on WEB-37. A card that needs you keeps its heavier left edge.		Owner, 7 Nov (D18): the avatar shows the run; it replaces 4c B2’s run words on the card. B4.
9Finished columns fold to a strip
Verified is a finishing column, so it folds; a click opens it as a full column. The working columns keep the room, also beside the conversation.		4c B1, kept, now by state rather than by name.
10One filled button: New task
＋ New task makes a Bug in Reported, the type’s first column (the Backlog state). Talk about this board opens a conversation that can add and order tasks.		D11: a new task starts in Backlog. B6.
11A card opens the task as a sheet over the board
The board stays behind it with its scroll kept; the task has one address. The task page is Task.		4c B4, kept.

Left open

  1. Dropping a card on a filtered board (some cards hidden): it goes straight after the visible card above it in the project’s order. Recommended: yes, the simplest rule that keeps one rank. recommended
Why.
  • 4c B1–B4 brought across: search, folded strips, one card layout, the sheet over the board. Changed: the board no longer owns columns (they are the type’s), the Columns / Timeline switch goes (Timeline has its own place), and no column starts work.
  • R0b’s board had a Ready column that started work and Run Ready in order; both now lead to the Runs page’s ▶ Start (Workroom), which follows the rank set here. The board only arranges.

What each number is, and why

1Columns, open: the four ways in one menu
Task state; a type’s own columns (only types whose columns differ from the four states: Task and Epic, still plain here, are reached by Task state and the Type filter); a custom field, or ＋ New field… (Board by custom field); the execution state, marked read-only (Board by execution state). Each says what its columns will be.		Owner: “one board view … different ways to plan”. D3, BS2.
2Built in
Task state and Execution are on every project and can’t be deleted or renamed; a changed view of them saves as a new board (Saving a board).		D3: “there is always a board for the task state and a board for the execution state”.
3A card names its type and its column
Here the columns are states, so each card says which type it is and which of its type’s columns it is in: Feature request · Testing is In progress.		D10: the state follows from the column; this board is the view across types.
4Dropping a card in a state puts it in its type’s column for that state
WEB-46 (Feature request, Submitted) dropped on To do goes to Accepted, the type’s column for To do. The slot says which column before you let go.		D5, D10, and Task types’s default column per state.
5A Type filter, on boards that span types
Only here and on custom-field and execution boards; a type’s own board has one type already.		B5 lists sprint, epic, agent; a board across types needs one more. Left open 2.
6An epic is a card like any other, never run
It shows its progress (3 of 7 done) and its managing agent with no ring (an epic never runs), and no Run in its ⋯; the Runs page’s ▶ Start passes over it.		D12, T10 (approved in 4b: an epic has no runs).
7One order across types
Dragging a card up or down here sets the same project-wide rank as on every other board; the Runs page’s ▶ Start (Workroom) follows it. Nothing on the board starts work.		D14; owner, 7 Nov: starting is on Runs.

Left open

  1. Dropping on a state with several columns of that type in it (e.g. Feature request has Building and Testing in In progress): the card goes to the type’s default column for that state, set in Task types. Recommended, so a drop never asks a question. recommended
  2. A Type filter on boards that span types (task state, custom field, execution). Recommended: yes. recommended
Why.
  • Project Tasks, the default board that held tasks on no other board, is replaced by this built-in board (Q5): a task needs no board.
  • The Columns menu is the one place a person chooses how to look at the work, so a new kind of board is not a new screen.

Not started · Waiting · Running · Needs you · Failed · Finished, set by the system from each task’s latest run. Marked Read-only in the header and in the Columns menu.		D2, D3: the execution state is the system’s; no one sets it by hand. R0e drew it first.
2No drag; why is said where you try
A card here has no drag; pressing to drag shows the tooltip, not a message in the page. Rank is still the order inside each column, changed on any other board.		Standing rule: a refusal known in advance is greyed with why. Q3: the Execution board is not dragged.
3Each card acts for its column
Running: Stop, Open in Runs. Needs you: Answer on the card. Failed: Run again on the card. Not started: Run. Move to › is greyed with why.		B4, RU1, RU4: act without leaving the board.
4The ring matches the column; the words are on hover
Each card’s agent avatar carries the same ring as everywhere (D18); hovering gives the words, here “Waiting · 2nd for Writer, after WEB-12”: one task at a time per agent, in rank order. No run text on the cards.		Owner, 7 Nov (D18). RU2, R5 (why a run waits).
5Not started is not a queue
No run button on this column either. Work starts on the Runs page (Workroom), from each agent’s ▶ Start or ▶ Start all agents; a single card runs from its ⋯. This board only shows what the runs are doing.		Owner, 7 Nov: starting moves to Runs; D6.
6Every card names its type and column
So a person sees what the plan says while the run says something else (e.g. Bug · Fixing, Running).		D2: three kinds of state, never derived from each other.

Left open

  1. Tasks with no runs and no agent sit in Not started like any other; Run on them is greyed with “Give it an agent first”. Recommended. recommended
Why.
  • A board grouped by execution lets someone planning a sprint or an epic see what the agents are doing with exactly those tasks; Runs (Workroom) shows every run, with replies and routine runs too.
  • Making it read-only keeps D2: the plan is changed on the plan’s boards, never by dragging a run.

What each number is, and why

1Type, first in the header
Changing it keeps the state: the task lands on the new type’s default column for that state (here Feature request → Accepted). An epic can’t be chosen while the task has an agent (greyed with why).		D10 (“changing a task’s type keeps its state”); D12.
2The column, by name only
The menu lists the type’s columns, nothing else; the task state behind them never shows here (it is defined in Settings › Task types). The execution state is a separate fact, set by the system, shown at 6.		D2 (three kinds of state, never derived); D5, D10. T0’s Launch plan › In progress goes: no board owns the task (D3).
3Sprint, by name only
One sprint of the project’s series, or none. Its dates show only in Sprints (Sprints), not on the task.		D8, D13.
4Order is never shown as a number
The task’s place in the project’s order is hidden, as in Jira, Linear and Trello: you change it by dragging on any board, or with ⋯ › Move to top / Move to bottom. No Rank field.		D14; owner, 7 Nov: “the rank should probably not take up a slot … a hidden number during ordering”.
5The project’s custom fields
One row per single-select field; none means it is on no board whose columns are that field.		D4: views only, never the state.
6The agent, its ring, and the run in words
The agent’s avatar with the run’s ring (D18), and here, unlike a list, the words beside it: Writer · Not started, Running · 1 min, Needs your okay. The filled button follows: Run ▾, Stop, Review. One task is started here (Run now, Run at…) or from a card’s ⋯; a whole agent from its station on Runs; every agent from ▶ Start all agents….		D18; D6 (only an explicit act starts work). T0 had the execution state as words alone.

Left open

  1. Turning a task with runs into an epic. Recommended: not allowed (greyed, “It has runs; an epic is never run”). An epic made from a task with no runs is fine.
Why.
  • T0 approved 6 Nov; T9 (⋯ menu) and T10 (epic page) approved and kept. T9’s Make this an epic leaves the ⋯ menu: the Type field does it.
  • Owner, 7 Nov: “done always means done … they all mean different things”.
  • Run ▾ holds Run now and Run at… (D6; R0h: Run at… is today’s start time).

12Nothing needs you, nothing running, nothing in line. Start is greyed: “No task is ready for Tester”.
6 Every run, finished or not, is on Runs ›, the project’s history (Project Runs).

What each number is, and why

1Counts, about running only
Needs you (a filter, 2), Running, Waiting, Finished today, and what today’s runs cost. Running, Waiting and Finished today open the project’s Runs (Project Runs) filtered to that state.		RU1–RU3. The Tasks list no longer counts run states (P1); these counts live here only (D9).
2Needs you: a notification bar on its agent’s card
Each approval, question or failure (from a task, a routine run or a reply in a conversation) is a full-width bar at the bottom of the card, below its panels, one per item, stacked: an attention mark, the avatar ringed to match (D18), the item in one line (key, title, what happened), and its one action at the right end (Run again, Review, Answer). A card with a bar has a heavy edge; a card with nothing needing you has no bar. The Needs you number stays in the band, and the count card at the top narrows the page to those agents without reordering them. A failed run does not hold its agent’s line: the line moves on and the failure waits as a bar (decided 7 Nov).		Owner, 7 Nov: “needs you should be attached to the agent”; “lift the needs you up as a notification bar”; “maybe it’s at the bottom … it already happened, so the user would want to see the current work instead.” The heavy edge and the Needs you number in the band say it at a glance. RU1.
3One scorecard per agent: the Execution view, by agent
Each agent of the project is one card across the whole row, like a team’s scorecard: a band on top (who it is, its status, its numbers, Start and Stop) then three panels side by side, the current work first: At work · In line · Finished today; any Needs you bars (2) come last, at the card’s bottom. A section with nothing in it shrinks to one line of words under the panels, so the card stays compact. No table header, no grid lines. It is the execution side of Board by execution state (the board grouped by execution state), turned to show who is doing what. Five agents drawn, to show it at scale.		Owner, 7 Nov: “make it look like a hero card for the entire row … a sports team score card: you see everything on the card.” RU1, RU2; Board by execution state.
4In line, with why each waits
Rank order; every line says why it isn’t running and what starts it: next after the run at work, its Run at… time, the site’s runs at once all busy, the site not answering.		R5, adapted: the pulse, the switch and the throttle are removed (D6).
5Routine runs are runs
A routine’s run shows on its agent’s card (here asking a question, as a Needs you bar at the bottom of the card) and in every list, named by the routine and its run number. It is not in the agent’s line of tasks (Left open 1).		RU5, D15.
6Runs: the history, on its own page
The Workroom shows only what is live and today. Every run, finished or not, is on the project’s Runs (Project Runs); a card’s Finished today ›, a task’s Runs tab and a run’s links lead there.		D19 (owner, 7 Nov): the live view is the Workroom; Runs is the history.
7The order of tasks is the board’s
In line follows the project’s one rank; Runs never reorders tasks. The link opens a board, where the rank is arranged by dragging.		D14 (one rank), D1.
8Start all agents… and Stop every run…
▶ Start all agents…, the page’s one filled button, does what each card’s Start does for every agent, after one confirm grouped by agent (Starting work). Stop every run…, outlined, asks once (Workroom states). Boards have no run buttons; a single task still runs from its page or a card’s ⋯.		Owner, 7 Nov. D6; R8, adapted.
9The band: who, and Start / Stop
The ringed avatar (40 px, D18), the name, the agent’s role, its status in words (At work · 1 min, Free, Needs you · 2), then ▶ Start (the agent’s ready tasks: in a To do column, not yet run, with that agent, one at a time in rank order, after a confirm, Starting work) and ■ Stop (its running task stops, its waiting ones go back to Not started), each greyed with why.		Owner, 7 Nov. RU2, RU4; D14.
10The ring on an agent’s avatar (D18)
Next to a task’s run, the agent’s avatar carries the execution state: dotted and still for Waiting, a turning arc for Running, a dot for Needs you, “!” for Failed, none for Not started and Finished; words on hover. It replaces the state chip; a reason or a time stays as the row’s second line. The card’s avatar is ringed while the agent is at work.		Owner, 7 Nov (D18).
WNot started / Finished: no ringWWaiting: dotted, stillWRunning: turning arcWNeeds you: dotW!Failed: !
11Drag cards to reorder the agents
⋮⋮ on each card; the order is kept for the project (Left open 2). Needs you never reorders them on its own.		Owner, 7 Nov.
12A quiet agent is one band
An agent with nothing in any section is a single band (who, numbers, Start) with one line saying so. Researcher, free but with finished runs, keeps its Finished panel.		Owner, 7 Nov: scales to many agents.
13The numbers, like a scoreboard
Big numbers on the band: Needs you, Ready, In line, Runs today, and what today cost.		Owner, 7 Nov: “you see everything on the card.” RU3.

Brought across, and what changed

Kept from R1 option B: one place per agent (now a scorecard), the header’s Stop; every run as a list moves to its own page, Runs (Project Runs, D19). Changed: stations side by side become one scorecard per agent across the row, with a band of who, status, numbers and Start/Stop over its sections, so many agents scale downwards (owner, 7 Nov); Needs you is a notification bar at the bottom of each card, below its panels, and its count card filters to those agents; Start every waiting task replaced by Start per agent and Start all agents…, both asking first; Automation gone from the menu, Routines in its place; cost per run and per day (RU3); Kind filter from R4 with Routine runs; R5’s reasons cut to those that still exist.

Left open

  1. Does a routine run or a reply wait in its agent’s line? Recommended: no. An agent’s line is its started tasks (spec §4); a routine run or a reply runs beside it, limited only by the site’s runs at once (5). recommended
  2. Is the agents’ order kept per project or per person? Recommended: per project, the same for everyone, as task types and their columns are the project’s (D16) and as N5 keeps such orders on the project. recommended
  3. Does an agent’s Stop ask first? Recommended: yes, one short question naming the run and how many waiting tasks go back to Not started, as Stop every run does. recommended
Why.
  • RU1–RU5; D1 (Tasks plan, Runs carry out), D6 (explicit starts only), D14 (one rank), D15 (routine runs), D18 (rings), D19 (Workroom and Runs); Board by execution state.
  • Your words: “it should read like showing the agent being at work” (6 Nov); “needs you should be attached to the agent” (7 Nov).

What each number is, and why

1One plain reason per waiting run
Next after the agent’s run at work; its Run at… time (with Run now); the site’s runs at once all busy; the site not answering. Each ends with what starts it.		R5; RU2 (why it waits). The pulse, the throttle, the queue limit and the automation switch are removed (D6, spec §8), so their reasons go.
2Stop every run… asks once
A centred dialog with the count, the agents and what happens to their tasks: waiting ones go back to Not started (decided 7 Nov); Stop 4 runs is the dialog’s one filled button. With nothing running the header button is greyed with “Nothing is running”.		R8, kept; RU4. Stopping everyone’s work at once is the one action here that can’t be undone.
3Nothing has run yet
The counts read 0, every agent is a single band with its numbers and Start, and one sentence says how work starts: tasks in a To do column with an agent, then Start. Each card says how many are ready; Start with none ready and every Stop are greyed with why.		The empty-list rule; D6; owner, 7 Nov.
4Phone: one agent per screen
Start all agents and Stop every run at the top; then one agent at a time, in the project’s agent order: its card’s band on top (who, status, numbers, Start and Stop), its three panels stacked (At work, In line, Finished today), then its Needs you bars at the bottom. Swipe or ‹ › for the next; the Needs you card narrows the agents to those that need you.		Panels side by side don’t fit a phone; this is the only layout that changes. Owner, 7 Nov.

Brought across, and what changed

R5 kept, with the automation and throttle reasons dropped and Run at… added. R8 kept for Stop; Start every waiting task becomes Start all agents…, which asks first (Starting work).
Why.
  • R5 and R8 (brought across); D6; RU2, RU4.

What each number is, and why

1What will run, in order
The agent’s ready tasks: in a To do column (any type’s column that sits in To do), not yet run, with that agent; numbered in the project’s rank order, with type and column. Each has a tick; untick to leave it out.		Owner, 7 Nov; D14 (rank is the order), D10 (a column sits in one task state).
2What can’t run, and why
Tasks that would otherwise be ready are named with the reason: an epic is never run (D12); a task with a Run at… time waits for it. Nothing here has a tick.		Owner, 7 Nov: the confirm names what can’t run. A refusal known in advance is said where it applies.
3Start, with the count
The dialog’s one filled button says how many will start; with every tick cleared it is greyed (“Nothing ticked”). The tasks join the agent’s line; the first starts at once if the agent is free.		D6: nothing starts without an explicit act.

The same list for every agent of the project, under each agent’s name, with what it is on now; an agent with nothing ready says so.		Owner, 7 Nov: Start all is the same for every agent, one confirm grouped by agent.
5Can’t run, for all
As (2), plus a task with no agent, which no station can take.		Owner, 7 Nov.

Brought across, and what changed

R8’s Start every waiting task becomes Start all agents… with this confirm. Board run buttons (R0b’s Run Ready in order and its successor) are gone.

Left open

  1. Is a task already waiting in the line listed again? Recommended: no; the confirm lists only tasks not yet run, and the line shows the rest. recommended
  2. Does a ready task added after Start join the line on its own? Recommended: no. Start takes the tasks ticked at that moment; a task made ready later waits for the next Start (D6: nothing starts without an explicit act). recommended
Why.

7 A project with no sprints.

What each number is, and why

1The current sprint
Its number, dates and days left; See Sprint 4 on a board › opens the board (Board) filtered to Sprint 4, grouped however you last grouped it.		D8, D13: a sprint is the project’s time box; a sprint board is any board filtered to it (B5).
2How it is going, by task state
One bar by task state across every type; Done always means done. What runs now is one line linking to the Workroom, not a count here; in the list each task’s agent is ringed with its execution state (D18), with no state chip.		D2: task state and execution state kept apart; P1 (Tasks competing with Runs); D18 (owner, 7 Nov).
3Finish sprint…
A sprint ends only when someone (or an agent’s finish_sprint) finishes it; past its last day the page says “ended 2 days ago” beside it. Asks where the unfinished go (Planning and finishing a sprint); finishes at once when all are done. ⋯ holds Rename.		B6, brought across; decided 7 Nov.
4Upcoming sprints
The next sprints in the series, each with its dates and how many tasks are planned in it; Plan it › opens planning (Planning and finishing a sprint). The page’s one filled button plans the next sprint.		S5: planning takes tasks from Backlog or To do into a sprint. Owner, 7 Nov: “only see upcoming sprints”.
5Past sprints, out of the way
Not on the page: one quiet link at its foot, Past sprints (12) ›, opens them as a simple list (dates, what was done, what moved on), newest first; each opens its tasks. They are kept, as the spec says.		Owner, 7 Nov: “can we only see upcoming sprints not past sprints?” B6.
6One series, one length
The series’ length and start day are set here, once for the project.		D13 (one series per project, one cadence for every type).
7No sprints yet
Says what sprints are and how to start; nothing else is needed for a project that doesn’t use them.		The empty-list rule; sprints are optional.

Brought across, and what changed

B6’s sprint bar (name, dates, days left, Finish, Rename) becomes this page, with Past sprints moved behind one link (owner, 7 Nov); its columns go, because a sprint has none of its own (D8). The board’s Not in a sprint column is replaced by the Backlog and To do lists in planning (Planning and finishing a sprint).

Left open

  1. How many upcoming sprints show? Recommended: the next two, made from the series’ length; either can be planned, as drawn. recommended
Why.
  • D8, D13; spec §5 (a task is in at most one sprint); B6 brought across.

What each number is, and why

1Backlog and To do, on the left
Every type’s Backlog and To do tasks in rank order, with search, Type, Epic and ＋ Filter, and an optional Group by epic. Its own scrollbar: a long backlog scrolls here without moving the sprint.		S5: planning takes tasks from Backlog or To do. D14 (rank). Owner, 7 Nov: two panels side by side, not Jira’s stack (“I have to scroll too far”).
2Sprint 5, on the right
Its dates and task count, and a goal line you edit in place (“Launch pages ready for review”).		D13.
3Planning commits Backlog tasks
A Backlog task dropped into the sprint moves to To do (its type’s default column for To do), said once in the panel’s header.		N1; D11 (decided 7 Nov).
4Ask Writer to plan it
A quiet link in the page header, beside Done planning: opens the project’s conversation, where the agent moves tasks here with its tools. Nothing sits below the panels, which run to the foot of the screen.		B6 (talk the board through); spec §8 (agents’ tools on sprints).
5Finish sprint…
Done tasks stay recorded; the rest go to the next sprint or none; their task state and column don’t change. With all done, it finishes without asking.		B6, brought across; U4b (Finish sprint leaves the task state alone).
6Drag, and you can see it
Every row has a ⋮⋮ handle; a row being dragged lifts with a shadow and travels between the panels. Dragging works both ways (back to the Backlog) and within Sprint 5.		Owner, 7 Nov: make dragging obvious.
7Where it lands
A dashed slot in Sprint 5 shows the place and says what will happen (3rd, moves to To do). The order within the sprint is the project’s rank.		D14: one rank, so ordering here orders every board.
8Load per agent
Tasks per agent in the sprint as small bars (Writer 4 · Reviewer 2 · Researcher 0). No estimates: load is a count of tasks.		Owner, 7 Nov: no estimates.
9The epics it moves forward
Each epic with tasks in the sprint, and how many.		D12; T5.
10⋯ on a row: without a mouse
Add to Sprint 5 or Back to Backlog (and move up or down), for the keyboard and the phone. No checkboxes, no Add button.		Accessibility; owner, 7 Nov.
11Each panel scrolls on its own
A visible scrollbar in each; the Backlog runs long below (rows cut off at the foot).		Owner, 7 Nov.
12Done planning, and no Save
Each move is the plan, as on a board, so there is nothing to save or cancel. Done planning (outlined) goes back to Sprints; no filled button, since nothing is created.		Chosen over no button at all, so the way back is plain.

Brought across, and what changed

B6’s Finish dialog kept, with No sprint for Not in a sprint and one sentence that the task state stays. Planning is new: today a task enters a sprint by being dragged onto the sprint board; here it is two scrolling lists side by side, not the stacked layout Jira uses.
Why.
  • D11, D13, D14; N1; spec §5; B6.

7 New routine: the same page, empty; it starts on, and its first run is at the next time.

What each number is, and why

1The same band as its card
Name, agent (ringed while its run is going, D18), on behalf of the last person who changed it, the switch, ▶ Run now, ⋯; and a heavy edge while something needs you.		Routines; D15.
2How it’s going, and when
The strip of its last runs (■ finished, ✕ failed, • needed you), the counts and the average cost, then the schedule in words and when it fires next. A run that is asking shows as the notification bar under it.		RT2; RU3; owner, 7 Nov.
3Instructions
What the agent does each time, in the one Markdown editor (8). Creating tasks is something the instructions may ask for.		D15; D7 (a routine creates tasks only through its agent’s tools, never by default).
4On or off, and Run now
The switch, and Run now: fires it once outside the schedule, as a run you started.		D15; D6: a person’s explicit act. See Left open 1.
5Its runs
Every firing as one run: its mark, what it did (and the tasks it made), how long, cost; each opens the run (A run); All in Runs › opens the project’s Runs filtered to this routine (Project Runs).		RT2; RU3; D19.
6Details
Agent, the schedule (read back in words with the next three times, then its preset, cron expression and timezone, and ✎ Change), the model (the agent’s default unless chosen), on whose behalf (the last person who changed it; not editable), where.		D15; D22.
7New routine
The same page empty; Create routine is its one filled button; Ask the agent to help write it as on a task.		RT1; T8 (New task is a page shaped like the task page).
8One Markdown editor
The instructions use the same editor as a task’s description and comments: Write and Preview, the toolbar (bold, italic, link, list, code), the same box. Preview on the routine’s page until you click into it, Write on New routine.		D21 (owner, 7 Nov): one Markdown editor everywhere text is written; Task.
9Repeats: presets in words
Every N minutes · Every N hours · Daily at · Weekdays at (one or more times) · Weekly on (day chips) · Monthly on day N · Monthly on the first or last weekday, each with its fields. Every N minutes refuses fewer than 5, said under the field.		D22 (owner, 7 Nov): cron plus a timezone, so anything cron allows. The 5-minute floor is a refusal known in advance, so it sits on the control, not in a banner.
10Advanced: a cron expression
A text field for anything the presets don’t cover (e.g. 0 9,15 * * 1-5); picking a preset fills it in. A step under 5 minutes is refused on the field, with why.		D22.
11Timezone
The routine’s timezone, from your own by default.		D22.
12Read back, always
Under the builder, always: the schedule in plain words and the next three run times, so a cron expression can be checked before it is saved.		D22; RT1.
13The page is its edit screen
Every part changes in place, with the same fields and layout as New routine: the name (✎), the agent, the instructions in the Markdown editor, the schedule, on/off. No separate edit page.		Owner, 7 Nov; T8 (new and edit consistent).
14Changing the schedule, in place
✎ Change opens the schedule builder where the schedule was, with the new time read back and the next three runs; Cancel and Save change sit under it (Save change is the filled button while editing).		Owner, 7 Nov; D22.
15Saving asks first
A small centred dialog: “Save this change? This routine will now run on your behalf (Sam Okafor), not Kai’s.” Cancel / Save. It shows only when the change moves whose behalf it runs on.		N6; D15: a routine runs on behalf of the last person who changed it.

Brought across, and what changed

New screen. Replaces the task page’s Start time › Make it a routine (04 · 46): a routine is no longer made from a task (D7). Since the first draw: the band and run strip from the Routines cards (owner, 7 Nov).

Left open

  1. Run now: may a person fire a routine outside its schedule? Recommended: yes; it is an explicit act (D6), shown as a run started by you. recommended
  2. The next firing comes while the last run is still going. Recommended: that firing is skipped and listed in its runs as Skipped · run 14 was still running, so runs never pile up. recommended
  3. Who may make and change routines? Recommended: as for tasks today, anyone who may work in the project; changing it makes it run on their behalf (decided), and saving asks first (15, N6). recommended
Why.
  • D6, D7, D15, D18, D19; RT1–RT2.

UI: what the wireframes leave open Approved

open items · merged

What this asks. The three designers left 40 items open. Merged here: seven needed you, all decided on 7 Nov; the rest are taken as drawn because they follow from the spec or are plain defaults.

Needs you

#QuestionRecommendedPages
N1Does planning a Backlog task into a sprint move it to To do? The spec says moving to To do is deciding to do it; putting it in a sprint is arguably that decision.Decided: yes (owner, 7 Nov): adding a Backlog task to a sprint moves it to To do, its type’s default To do column.Planning and finishing a sprint
N2A task added from a board column: does it start in that column, or in Backlog? The board and planning designers drew it differently.Decided (owner, 7 Nov): in that column, at the bottom of the rank; ＋ New task in the header starts in Backlog.Board, New task
N3Does a failed run hold its agent’s line?Decided: no (owner, 7 Nov): the failure waits under Needs you and the agent takes its next task.Workroom
N4Stop every run: does it also take waiting tasks out of line?Decided: yes (owner, 7 Nov): back to Not started; nothing more starts until someone runs it.Workroom states
N5Are saved boards the project’s only, or can a person keep their own views?Decided (owner, 7 Nov): the project’s only; a per-person view is too complex for now.Saving a board
N6Who may make or change a routine, and on whose behalf does it run after a change? A routine runs with someone’s access.Decided (owner, 7 Nov): anyone who may work in the project may make one; a routine always runs on behalf of the last person who changed it (“the safest option for accountability”), and the save says so first.A routine and New routine
N7Does a sprint end on its own date?Decided (owner, 7 Nov): finished only explicitly; it stays current, shown as overdue after its date (“some sprints may continue over time because of delays”).Sprints

Taken as drawn

FromTaken as drawn (recommended, obvious)
Board a drop on a filtered board goes after the visible card above; a drop on a state lands on the type’s default column; boards across types get a Type filter; anyone in the project may add a field option; Run greyed on a card without an agent; “Current sprint” follows to the next; leaving an unsaved view asks nothing; Boards opens the list; no board archive; on a phone, Save as board in ⋯.
PlanningDragging rows changes rank only while sorted by Rank; the run marker stays on Tasks and Your tasks; Move to To do on a selection; custom fields listed in Settings and made from the Columns menu; a type with open tasks can’t be archived, only a never-used type deleted; moving a column to another state only from its ⋯ with a dialog; a task with runs can’t become an epic; an epic never moves column by itself; a new task goes to the bottom of the rank; “yours” = its For is you (ADR-0095).
RunningRoutine runs and replies don’t wait in an agent’s line; the Runs page is reached from the panel and Home, not the rail; it shows your runs by default; a reply opens its conversation; a stopped run reads “Stopped by …” and its task goes back to Not started; only the next sprint is planned ahead; routines get Run now; a firing while the last run is going is skipped and listed; an across-projects Routines list stays.
LeadThe three sets now share the app’s real rail (Home · Chat · Your space · Projects · Boards · Tasks · Workspaces · Routines · Agents · Library; Runs and Notifications in its foot). Column colours: the board designer’s. Custom fields in Settings › Custom fields (planning) and from the Columns menu (board): both.
